Topic at a glance
Information Technology Act s. 67B — Statutory provision (Information Technology Act s. 67B) is a registered section in Cyber Law. Information Technology Act s. 67B — Statutory provision (Information Technology Act s. 67B) is governed by Information Technology Act, 2000, allied rules, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 where applicable, BSA 2023 and constitutional privacy principles. identify the date, technology, applicable IT Act provision, data regime, intermediary rule and evidence law; distinguish struck-down provisions from current offences.

Provenance, purpose and doctrinal foundation
The topic exists to organise a legally enforceable rule, doctrine or professional procedure. Read the statutory text, constitutional setting, institutional purpose and binding authorities together. The correct analysis begins with the legal question and avoids replacing the governing enactment with a generic textbook summary.

Textual anatomy and operative test
1. Identify the governing enactment, section, article, rule, doctrine or professional standard named by the topic.
2. Deconstruct definitions, conditions precedent, exceptions, provisos, explanations, jurisdictional limits and remedies.
3. Distinguish the topic from its nearest neighbour: IT Act s. 4 — Legal recognition of electronic records; IT Act s. 10A — Validity of contracts formed through electronic means; IT Act s. 43 — Penalty and compensation for damage to computer system.
4. Apply the rule to the record and state which fact satisfies or fails each ingredient.

Courtroom and evidentiary roadmap
Competent forum: the designated cyber-crime police and criminal court, adjudicating officer, civil court, High Court under Articles 226/227, or competent data-protection and regulatory forum. the complainant or prosecution must establish the digital act, attribution, unauthorised access or communication, causation and statutory ingredients; electronic records require BSA s. 63 foundation where applicable. Where electronic records are relied upon, apply BSA 2023 s. 63 and the applicable burden provisions without treating electronic admissibility as proof of the ultimate fact. Identify limitation, notice, maintainability, alternative remedy and the exact relief sought.

cases.name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Court reviewed restrictions on online speech under the Information Technology Act.
cases.issue: Whether IT Act s. 66A impermissibly restricted constitutional speech.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 66A was vague and overbroad and violated Article 19(1)(a); it was not saved by Article 19(2).
cases.holding: Section 66A was struck down in its entirety.
cases.relevance: Use only as historical status; do not present s. 66A as a current offence.

cases.name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
cases.facts: The Court examined the statutory method for proving electronic records.
cases.issue: Whether electronic records can be admitted without the applicable certificate route.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Electronic records must satisfy the special statutory proof requirements applicable to computer outputs.
cases.holding: The Court reaffirmed the certificate discipline for electronic evidence.
cases.relevance: Use with BSA s. 63 and digital-record admissibility.

cases.name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Constitution Bench considered privacy as a constitutional right in the digital and modern State.
cases.issue: Whether privacy is protected as a Fundamental Right.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Privacy is intrinsic to dignity, liberty and Part III, subject to legality, legitimate aim, proportionality and procedural safeguards.
cases.relevance: Use for surveillance, data protection and informational privacy.
